common_name: Marseilles Black Fig (Marseilles Black VS, MBVS)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Marseilles Black is self-fertile and needs no caprification, but its thin, sugar-rich skin is more prone to splitting in extended wet spells than closed-eye Gulf Coast selections.

directions: Marseilles Black (also traded as Marseilles Black VS or MBVS) is a self-fertile common-type fig valued by collectors for its deep purple-black skin and intensely sweet, dark red interior, with a flavor many growers compare to Black Madeira despite ripening earlier in the season. Early-twentieth-century university fruit trials in Maryland and Louisiana found it among the most productive figs tested, though its fruit size was judged too small for commercial sale, which has kept it largely a dooryard and collector variety rather than a nursery staple. It performs best where summers are hot, since the thin skin and rich sugar content that make it so flavorful also leave it more prone to splitting and souring in humid, rainy weather than dedicated closed-eye Gulf Coast cultivars. Grow it in full sun with good drainage, and expect a modest but well-flavored crop even from a young tree.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Dark Portuguese is a self-fertile common-type fig that ripens early for a dark-skinned variety, which lets it beat some of the worst late-summer Gulf Coast humidity before splitting sets in.

directions: Dark Portuguese is a common-type fig traced to the central mountains of Portugal and long circulated among American fig collectors through cutting trades rather than retail nurseries. It produces small-to-medium fruit with a deep purple-black skin and a red interior carrying an intense berry flavor alongside a milder floral sweetness. Self-fertile like other common figs, it needs no second tree or caprification, and Gulf South growers trade it alongside other collector varieties for its early ripening window. Plant in full sun with well-drained soil and expect a single late-summer main crop rather than a significant breba crop.
sources: Ben B Seattle — Plant Collector blog

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Takoma Violet is self-fertile and often grown in containers where hard freezes are a concern, since it tolerates cold better than many Mt. Etna-type figs.

directions: Takoma Violet is a Mt. Etna-type common fig discovered in a dooryard planting in Takoma Park, Maryland in 2001 and since spread hand-to-hand through fig-collector cutting trades across the South. It bears a long season of medium-small, violet-skinned, jammy-fleshed figs, from a modest breba crop in early summer through a heavier main crop into fall, and growers from the Gulf Coast to the mid-Atlantic rate its flavor among the best of the Etna-type figs. Its fruit holds up reasonably well through rainy spells compared to many open-eye varieties, though Gulf South growers still see better split resistance from dedicated closed-eye selections. Self-fertile and needing no caprification, it grows well in full sun and well-drained soil.
